column2: The wise do not know the other world by direct sight; without transgressing the scriptures one who wishes to prosper should have faith.
The learned man should perform rites for ancestors and gods, practise the duties, sacrifice duly, and follow the triple aim.
This world, sinking in the deep ocean of Time, whose great crocodiles are old age and death, no one comprehends.
Many physicians, studying the science of life, are seen to be flooded with diseases, with their equipment.
Drinking decoctions and various kinds of ghee, they do not pass beyond death, as the great ocean does not pass its shore.
Those who know elixirs and apply them well are seen broken by old age, like trees by the best of elephants.
Likewise those endowed with austerity, devoted to Vedic study, givers and sacrificers, do not cross over old age and death.
Days do not return, nor months, nor years, for all beings that are born, nor fortnights, nor nights.
This man, impermanent, helplessly by Time certainly goes the long road frequented by all beings.
Either the body goes from the living, or the living being leaves the body; this is a meeting on the road with wives, other relatives and kinsmen.
No one ever gets lasting companionship even with his own body, how much less with anyone else.
Where is your father today, king, where your grandfather? You do not see them today, nor do they see you.
A man is not a seer of heaven or hell; the eye of the good is the scripture; follow that here, king.
One who has practised celibacy should beget offspring and sacrifice, free of envy, to be quit of debts to ancestors, gods and great sages.

He who is devoted to sacrifice, engaged in begetting offspring, having first been a celibate student, with his sides divided, worshipping heaven and this world, and then renouncing the heart's wound for the highest,
for a king rightly practising dharma and rightly collecting wealth, whose wheel is turning, fame grows in all worlds, moving and unmoving."

[Vyasa said:] Thus understanding, the king of Videha, with his reasons fulfilled, having taken the whole speech to heart, took leave of Ashma, pure in mind, and went to his own home, his grief calmed.
So you also, Achyuta, cast off grief; rise, equal to Shakra, come to joy; the earth has been won by you by kshatriya dharma; enjoy it, son of Kunti; do not despair.
[Arjuna said:] "The king of dharma, scorcher of foes, tormented by grief for his kinsmen, is sunk in an ocean of grief; comfort him, Madhava.
We have all been in doubt again, Janardana; you ought to dispel his grief, mighty-armed one."
Thus addressed by the great-souled Vijaya, Govinda, lotus-eyed Achyuta, turned to the king.
For Keshava, Govinda, was one whom the king of dharma could not transgress, and from boyhood he loved him more than Arjuna.
Taking his sandal-smeared arm, like a pillar of rock, Shauri, trying to console him, said:
His face shone, with fine teeth and lovely eyes, like a lotus wide open, awakened by the sun.

Having agreed, 'So be it,' those two sages honoured by the world went to King Srinjaya, son of Shvitya, and said this:
Then once the king said to the great souls, who had so come, highly pleased: 'This is my fair-complexioned daughter.
She is my only daughter and will attend upon you two, lovely, blameless of limb, endowed with good conduct, tender, a maiden like a lotus filament.'
Told 'Excellent, gentle one' by the two, the king commanded her: 'Daughter, serve the two Brahmanas as gods and fathers.'
Saying 'So be it' to her father, the maiden, devoted to dharma, honoured the two and served them as the king commanded.
By her service and her incomparable beauty, desire suddenly came swiftly into Narada's heart.
